checked_sources: Buzsáki, Anastassiou & Koch 2012 Nat Rev Neurosci 13(6):407-420 — full author manuscript (PMC4907333 via NCBI BioC)
Hämäläinen et al. 1993 Rev Mod Phys 65(2):413-497 — full PDF (Aalto repository)
evidence_location: Buzsáki 2012: sections 'Synaptic activity' and 'Spike contribution to the LFP' (Na+ spikes paragraph). Hämäläinen 1993: Sec. II.E 'Action potentials' (around p. 425-426, text accompanying Figs 16-17)
quote: strongest fields they generate are of short duration (<2 ms) and nearby neurons rarely fire synchronously
discrepancy: Split of support: 'tens of milliseconds' and the quadrupole/faster fall-off come only from Hämäläinen ('synaptic currents, which last tens of milliseconds ... action potentials ... 1 ms'; quadrupolar field 1/r^3 vs dipolar 1/r^2). Buzsáki says synaptic activity 'is often the most important source', not that it always dominates, and frames the <2 ms argument as why spikes 'were thought' not to contribute, adding that synchronous spikes can contribute substantially to high-frequency LFP components — a caveat the claim drops.
suggested_fix: Add '... although synchronous spiking can still contribute to high-frequency (>100 Hz) components' and attribute the duration/quadrupole statements to Hämäläinen et al. 1993.
bibliographic_issues: None; both citations match (RMP PDF header confirms Vol. 65, No. 2, April 1993).

checked_sources: Luck 2022, Applied ERP Data Analysis (LibreTexts), Chapter 8 landing page and sections 8.3, 8.5, 8.6, 8.9, 8.12
Jiang, Bian & Tian 2019 Sensors 19(5):987 — full text (PMC6427454)
Ronca et al. 2024 Bioengineering 11(10):1018 — full text (PMC11505294)
evidence_location: Luck ch. 8 intro ('large (often 200 µV)'); 8.3 ('uncorrected blinks are typically 100-200 µV in these [frontal] channels'); 8.5/8.6 (blink detection ±100 µV on VEOG-bipolar); 8.9 (step function, 50 µV); 8.12 (C.R.A.P.: ±200 µV absolute, 100-150 µV moving window). Jiang: sect. 2.2.1. Ronca: Introduction and Fig. 1
quote: a threshold of ±200 µV works well for most participants ... In most participants, we used a threshold between 100 and 150 µV.
discrepancy: Misattributed purpose: in Luck's chapter the ±200 µV absolute threshold and the 100-150 µV moving-window thresholds (sect. 8.12) are applied to all EEG channels to catch 'Commonly Recorded Artifactual Potentials' (large drifts, muscle bursts) after blinks were already rejected; blink detection itself used ±100 µV (then ±50 µV) on the bipolar VEOG channel (8.5-8.6) or a 50 µV step function (8.9). The conclusion about frontal blink size is supported directly (8.3: 'typically 100-200 µV'). 'Many times greater than EEG' is from Jiang 2019 ('The amplitude of EOG is generally many times greater than EEG'); Ronca 2024 says only 'much larger amplitudes'. Neither Jiang nor Ronca gives any µV figure.
suggested_fix: Rewrite as: 'Ocular artefact amplitude is many times greater than the EEG (Jiang 2019; Ronca 2024); uncorrected blinks are typically 100-200 µV at frontal channels, and practical ERP pipelines use blink thresholds of ±50-100 µV on bipolar VEOG, plus ±200 µV absolute and 100-150 µV moving-window thresholds for other large artefacts (Luck 2022, ch. 8).'
bibliographic_issues: None; LibreTexts URL resolves and Chapter 8 is 'Artifact Detection and Rejection'; Sensors and Bioengineering details match.

checked_sources: Jimenez & Ruifernández 1999 Dermatol Surg 25(4):294-298 — abstract via Europe PMC (PMID 10417585)
Van Neste 2004 Eur J Dermatol 14(1):28-32 — abstract via Europe PMC/PubMed (PMID 14965792)
evidence_location: Jimenez: Abstract, Results (65-85 FU/cm2, 124-200 hairs/cm2, 1.0-1.4 mm). Van Neste: Abstract, Results
quote: the average diameter of W hair (67.68 microm) exceeded that of P hair (57.41 microm)
discrepancy: Jimenez numbers all verbatim. The '57-68 µm' range is not a general female average: 57.41 µm is the mean for pigmented hairs and 67.68 µm for white (non-pigmented) hairs, pooled over top and occipital sites, in 24 Caucasian women (12 menopausal women complaining of hair loss/diffuse alopecia plus 12 controls). Jimenez's values are from 50 hair-transplant patients' occipital donor scalp.
suggested_fix: '...and in Caucasian women pigmented scalp hairs averaged ~57 µm and white hairs ~68 µm in diameter (Van Neste 2004).'
bibliographic_issues: Van Neste title is misquoted: PubMed gives '...according to pigmentation and scalp location during ageing', not '...in Caucasians'. Journal, year, volume 14(1) and pages 28-32 are correct; no DOI is listed in PubMed.
